title: Minimum Cost to Equalize Array
summary: Given an integer array nums and two integers cost1 and cost2, you can perform either of the following operations any number of times: - Choose an index i from nums and increase nums[i] by 1, with a cost of cost1.
statement: Given an integer array nums and two integers cost1 and cost2, you can perform either of the following operations any number of times: - Choose an index i from nums and increase nums[i] by 1, with a cost of cost1. - Choose two different indices i and j from nums and increase both nums[i] and nums[j] by 1, with a cost of cost2. Determine the minimum cost required to make all elements in the array equal, and return the result modulo 10^9 + 7.
constraints: nums is nonempty and contains nonnegative integers; both operation costs are positive.
A single operation increments one element; a pair operation increments two different elements.
Make every value equal at minimum cost and return that cost modulo 1,000,000,007.
hints: For a fixed target, the maximum legal pair count is limited by half the total deficit and by deficit outside the largest-deficit index.
Evaluate the current maximum and targets near the point where the largest deficit stops dominating; use singles when pairing is not cheaper.
pairs=min(totalDeficit//2,totalDeficit-largestDeficit); cost pairs and remaining singles; test the balance boundary and adjacent parities.
Fixed-target pairing is maximal when cheaper; cost is linear before balance and increasing after balance apart from parity, so the boundary neighborhood contains an optimum.
editorial: Fixed-target pairing is maximal when cheaper; cost is linear before balance and increasing after balance apart from parity, so the boundary neighborhood contains an optimum.

tests.explanation: With two elements every increment pair preserves their difference, so raise one by three single increments for cost fifteen.
Raise one and two together once, then raise the former one once more, reaching three for cost seven.
